messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Sat, Oct 6, 2012 at 7:40 AM, Bob <muen...@tennessee.edu> wrote:
> Hi All,
>
> I ddplyed the scale function in two, seemingly identical ways, but got a different result.
>
> First a bit of practice data:
>
> > library("plyr")
> > gender <- c("m","m","f","f")
> > score  <- 1:4
> > myDF <- data.frame(gender,score)
> > rm(gender,score)
> > myDF
>   gender score
> 1      m     1
> 2      m     2
> 3      f     3
> 4      f     4
> >
>
>
> Here's my goal, and this works just as I expected it to. "myscale" ignores the factor gender because numcolwise sets it up to do so.
>
> > myvars <- c("gender", "score")
> > myscale <- numcolwise(scale)
> > ddply(myDF[myvars], .(gender), myscale)
>   gender    score
> 1      f -0.70711
> 2      f  0.70711
> 3      m -0.70711
> 4      m  0.70711
> >

numcolwise() will apply the function it is passed to all numeric columns of the data frame. A direct call also works, as illustrated on the colwise() help page:

ddply(myDF, .(gender), numcolwise(scale))
  gender      score
1      f -0.7071068
2      f  0.7071068
3      m -0.7071068
4      m  0.7071068

...as does use of the colwise() function restricting application to the score variable:

ddply(myDF, .(gender), colwise(scale, .(score)))
  gender      score
1      f -0.7071068
2      f  0.7071068
3      m -0.7071068
4      m  0.7071068
>
> Now I'm trying to use scale instead. I can't simply replace myscale with scale since it tries to apply scale to gender:
> >
> > myvars <- c("gender", "score")
> > ddply(myDF[myvars], .(gender), scale)
> Error in colMeans(x, na.rm = TRUE) : 'x' must be numeric
> >

Correct. That's why colwise() and numcolwise() exist; both allow you to restrict the set of variables to which the function is to be applied.

>
> Here I remove gender from the "myvars" selection and pass it in as myDF$gender. This gives the correct values but why is the result not what I got in the first place?
> >
> > myvars <- c("score")
> > ddply(myDF[myvars], .(myDF$gender), scale)
>   myDF$gender       V1      V2
> 1           f -0.70711 0.70711
> 2           m -0.70711 0.70711
> >

myDF[myvars] is a one-column data frame but myDF$gender is a factor variable external to the input data frame. I imagine that some non-standard evaluation rules are applied in the background for this situation, but I don't have a ready explanation for the result. By design, the output must be a data frame, so perhaps a matrix is generated from the function call which is then coerced to a data frame on exit (?)

Dennis

messages.subject: Sorting a data frame with ddply instead of arrange
messages.subject_clean: Sorting a data frame with ddply instead of arrange
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I just stumbled across the fact that you can sort a data frame using ddply instead of arrange. If you use ddply and don't give it a function to apply, it simply splits the data frame by your variables and combines the pieces having done nothing to them. But since it does this in order, you've ended up sorting. In hindsight this is a bit obvious but I got a chuckle out of it so I thought I'd share. Example below.

Cheers,
Bob

> group <- sample(c("a","b"), 10, replace=TRUE)
> x <- rnorm(10)
> df <- data.frame(group,x)
> df
   group        x
1      a  1.79599
2      b -0.14837
3      a  0.16792
4      a -0.70860
5      b -0.52039
6      b -0.54596
7      b  1.71299
8      b  1.90250
9      b -0.37526
10     b -0.83634
> arrange(df, group, x)
   group        x
1      a -0.70860
2      a  0.16792
3      a  1.79599
4      b -0.83634
5      b -0.54596
6      b -0.52039
7      b -0.37526
8      b -0.14837
9      b  1.71299
10     b  1.90250
> ddply(df, .(group, x))
   group        x
1      a -0.70860
2      a  0.16792
3      a  1.79599
4      b -0.83634
5      b -0.54596
6      b -0.52039
7      b -0.37526
8      b -0.14837
9      b  1.71299
10     b  1.90250

(Maintainers of packages that depend on plyr have also been bcc'd)

new major changes, but I've fixed many of the small issues that have
accumulated in the last year since a major release. Since there are

me know if have you any problems.  It's easiest to get it with
devtools:

library(devtools)

Please let me know if you have any problems (esp. old code that no
longer works), any other comments or any feature requests.

Thanks!

Hadley

Sorry, my answer was wrong - it was a bug in plyr, and it's fixed in
the dev version:

> ddply(myDF[myvars], .(myDF$gender), scale)

  myDF$gender      score

1           f -0.7071068
2           f  0.7071068
3           m -0.7071068
4           m  0.7071068

FYI, you might also find the strip_splits function useful - it removes
all splitting variables.  This means you can do:

ddply(myDF, "gender", function(df) scale(strip_splits(df)))

and get what you want.  (It doesn't save much typing here but might in
more complicated cases)

colwise does this by default, so the minimum you need is

ddply(myDF, "gender", colwise(scale))

Hadley

I don't know if it will help, but I had a problem recently with a call to ddply that killed Rstudio as well. Unfortunately I don't have the code right now, since I modified it and was in a rush to finish a project and didn't have much time to look for bugs. I just used another approach. In any case, the code was something like this:

ddply(mydata, c("factor1", "factor2"), summarise, sum(id), .drop=T)

And whenever there was NA in one of the factors variables, it killed RStudio... And if I set .drop=F it didn't kill it. Or at least that was what I found at the moment.
Hope it helps,

Manoel

Here's the code. I just had a student try to replicate what I had done but this worked fine, so apparently it may be specific to my machine. On mine, any of the ddply statements below kills RStudio/RGui. On my student's machine none of them do but the previous bug is still present. Thanks, Bob

library("plyr")
gender <- c("m","m","f","f")
score  <- 1:4
myDF <- data.frame(gender,score)
rm(gender,score)
myDF

# Here's my goal, and this works:

myvars <- c("gender", "score")
myscale <- numcolwise(scale)

ddply(myDF[myvars], .(gender), myscale)

# I can't simply replace myscale with scale
# since  it tries to apply scale to gender
# which of couse is not numeric:

myvars <- c("gender", "score")

ddply(myDF[myvars], .(gender), scale)

# This gives the correct values but why
# is the result not what I got in the
# first place?

myvars <- c("score")
ddply(myDF[myvars], "myDF$gender", scale)

messages.subject_clean: Using dlply when a .variable has NAs
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I was apply a t.test by group using dlply when I got the cryptic message, "grouping factor must have exactly 2 levels." It turned out that the ".variable" was a factor with a missing value. I suppose dlply split that off as its own data frame with a single observation, preventing any of the other tests from running. I can manually delete values like this but I thought there must be something like "na.rm = TRUE" in plyr to avoid issues like this. Do I understand the situation and is there a plyr-based approach to dealing with it?  The code below demonstrates the problem.

Thanks,
Bob

group     <- rep(c("A", "B"), each  = 8)
treatment <- rep(c("A", "B"), times = 8)
score     <- 1:8
mydata    <- data.frame(group, treatment, score)
head(mydata)

myT <- function(df) {
  t.test(score ~ treatment, data = df)
}

# It works on the whole data frame:
myT(mydata)

# It also works by group:
dlply(mydata, .(group), myT)

# Set a factor value to missing
mydata$group[1] <- NA
head(mydata)

# It still works on the whole data frame:
myT(mydata)

# But it no longer works by group:
dlply(mydata, .(group), myT)

I think the plyr way to think about this is more about capturing
errors and continuing regardless.  With *lply, I'd approach it as
follows:

results <- dlply(mydata, .(group), failwith(NULL, myT))

# See where failures occur
ldply(results, is.null)

# Get rid of failures & extract stats
ok <- compact(results)
ldply(ok, is.null)
ldply(ok, function(x) data.frame(x[c("statistic", "p.value")]))

Hadley

people.ply <- ddply(people.melt, .(compare.1, compare.2, measure.strata, variable), summarize, mean.score=mean(value, na.rm=T))

for (k in 1:number.items) {
...
mean.score.compare.1 <- subset(people.ply, people.ply$compare.1==T & people.ply$variable==paste("item", k, sep=''))[, c("measure.strata", "mean.score")]
mean.score.compare.2 <- subset(people.ply, people.ply$compare.2==T & people.ply$variable==paste("item", k, sep=''))[, c("measure.strata", "mean.score")]
...

}
